en: The Buddhamānasūtra Chapter, also known as the Great Paritrāṇā Dhāraṇī, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying on the summit of Vajra Mountain in the kingdom of Kūṭāgāra.
He surveyed the ten directions, and they all appeared the color of fire.
At that time, the Tathāgata sighed deeply and gazed universally upon all sentient beings, seeing that they were entirely without distinction.
"How excellent! What means shall be used to save these sentient beings? he thought.
Having completed his contemplation,
[he beheld] all the Buddha-worlds and the spheres of all the bodhisattvas.
From the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven above down to the ten vajra-grounds and the palaces of Māra below, everything shook.
At that moment, all Buddhas of the past, present, and future appeared.
One should maintain right mindfulness and correct reflection. Furthermore,
there are bodhisattvas who abide within their own minds and remain unmoving.
Furthermore, there were various Vajrapāṇis leading their retinues and performing vajra-rites;
they did not remain in their seats but roamed throughout the ten directions. There were also various celestial beings, sages, and māras who fled in terror, finding no place of refuge.
At that time, ten Vajragarbha Bodhisattvas straightened their robes and addressed the Buddha,
saying: "World-Honored One, what is the significance of this present auspicious omen?"
"Is this an evil omen or a virtuous sign?
At that time, the Tathāgata merely reflected within himself and did not answer.
Then, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Vajrakaruṇā.
He addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"This sign is not auspicious.
Because the Buddha has now entered the samādhi of loving-kindness out of compassion, it is not called 'auspicious'."
Furthermore, purify your own minds and await what the Buddha shall proclaim.
At that time, there was also the Bodhisattva Guṇagañja,
who addressed Vajrakaruṇā, saying:
"What is called the Samādhi of Compassion? Vajrakaruṇā replied:
'It is precisely the place of rescue and gathering.'"
Excellent, excellent!
At that time, each of you should purify your body and mind for a brief moment.
He perceived that the mind of the Tathāgata pervades all sentient beings.
At that time, the Tathāgata arose from samādhi and addressed them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, sons of good family! Sentient beings are utterly submerged."
Do you not know all this?
I now see that sentient beings do not understand my Dharma nor know my mind;
they have not reached my limit and are possessed by Māra.
"How can they be saved? Who possesses the skillful means to protect them?
Who possesses the skillful means to gather in these sentient beings who are afflicted by this poison?
At that time, there were twenty quadrillion bodhisattvas.
All of them were great Dharma-princes who had received empowerment, possessing majestic power and sovereignty;
they came before the Buddha and said,
"World-Honored One, we possess the compassion of bodhisattvas."
The Buddha said, "This is not encompassed by loving-kindness.
Furthermore, there were as many Vajrapāṇis as there are grains of sand in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges Rivers;
each Vajrapāṇi held the strength of a champion of the four continents.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One, I am able to subdue it by my power.
The Buddha said, "Vajra, this cannot be subdued by power."
At that time, there was also the Mahādeva of all worlds,
who was able to transform his body into that of a Buddha and approach the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I possess mastery over transformations."
The Buddha said, "This is not something you can understand through deceptive illusions.
Among the assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Śrīguṇa who addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One, such are the Vajra-bodhisattvas and celestial seers."
"None are able to sustain or uphold it.
How may the Buddha now cause all sentient beings to escape this calamity?
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Bodhisattva Śuddhaguṇa, saying:
Only the Tathāgata’s Heart-Mind Core (Hṛdaya-hṛdaya) cannot reach it. Why is this?
Because it is able to cause all māras to give rise to great compassion.
Because it enables all phenomena to manifest according to their appropriate conditions;
because it enables all Buddhas to never be separated [from them];
and because it enables all Bodhisattvas to serve as one's retinue.
Because it enables all Vajradharas to bestow their majestic power;
because it enables the hosts of devas to constantly provide protection;
and because it causes the great yakṣas and rākṣasas to become an assembly that assists the Dharma.
Because it can cause all the great spirits and deities to give rise to joy;
because it enables those who maintain its recitation to become equal to the power of the Buddha;
and equal to the mind of the Buddha.
Because it is equal to the Buddha’s wisdom;
because it is equal to the Buddha’s majestic power;
and because it enables the practitioner to accomplish whatever they intend without fail.
Because it causes all obstacles and difficulties to be completely severed;
because Śakra and Brahmā kings constantly support it;
and because it enables all beings to proceed directly toward Bodhi without regression.
Because all worldly activities are clearly understood by oneself,
this extends even to the past, future, and present; to all worlds,
whether they possess supernatural powers or lack them, whether they possess wisdom or lack it, and whether they possess the virtuous or lack them.
Because they have all submitted and come to rest.
At that time, having heard this discourse, the great assembly all desired to listen and receive it.
Suddenly, within the great assembly, a radiance arose that surpassed a hundred thousand suns.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Real Virtue (Śrīguṇa) asked the Buddha,
"What is this light, and what are its causes and conditions?"
He replied: "This light of joy arises from the heart-center.
World-Honored One, you should know that this light is immeasurable and incomparable;
it cannot be praised, nor can it be authenticated."
Why is this? Because they are identical to all Buddhas in being without approval;
identical to all Tathāgatas in having nothing to be attained; because all marks are likewise not seen;
and because they guard their sense faculties without ever abandoning them.
Because it prevents all Māras and enemies from finding an opportunity,
and because it can block all the paths of the Māra-king,
for these reasons it is called the "Heart of Hearts."
At that time, the entire great assembly addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, based on the causes and conditions we have cultivated and the sublime teachings of the Buddha,
we have never before heard of such praise for meritorious virtues and such great majestic spiritual power."
We only pray that the Tathāgata will proclaim for us this stage of awakening realized through practice;
we only pray that we may cultivate it therein.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the bodhisattvas and all sons of good family:
"I shall now proclaim that there are ten kinds of sustenance for the realization and cultivation of the Buddha-ground, which will certainly bring accomplishment."
What are the ten? First is the maintenance of the mind:
being unimpeded regarding the Dharma, generating faith in the Buddha, and maintaining equanimity of mind.
He gives rise to loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and remains unattached to forms.
Second, he maintains the precepts without deficiency,
constantly abiding in meditative concentration and cultivating non-false speech.
Be generous to sentient beings and eliminate arrogance.
Third, do not commit evil deeds;
cultivate the precept of non-killing and do not consume unwholesome food.
Be careful not to praise yourself and do not look for the faults of others.
Fourth, do not give rise to contempt or disdain toward those who seek the Dharma;
protect against and guard against all evils within the Buddha's teachings.
Regard one's preceptors and teachers as one would one's own parents.
Fifth, if you practice the teachings of the precepts, be careful not to let them be lost;
observe all things, whether poor or wealthy, with an impartial mind.
One must maintain worldly conventions to accord with all people.
Sixth, one must always remain vigilant regarding the Buddha’s verses.
All dharmas that are practiced must be fully upheld.
Should anyone come to beg or request anything, one should grant it immediately according to their wishes;
take care not to examine whether their faculties are superior, middling, or inferior.
This is the seventh mudrā held by the deity.
There must be no impure conduct, and no binding of precepts at inappropriate times.
One must not employ them for the sake of fame or gain.
Furthermore, when practicing the Dharma, one must not abandon those who are not sentient beings.
Eighth, do not give rise to theft regarding anything that belongs to others; sever unrighteous evil and do not practice flattery.
Guard the essentials of the Buddha-dharma as you would your own life, and maintain no dualistic mind toward those who are noble or lowly.
Ninth, regarding those whom one rescues from the limits of suffering who lack sincerity:
truly, do not let your mind retreat;
do not disparage the Dharma yourself, nor cause others to disparage it.
One must sever one's own slanders and not cause others to slander;
one must be upright and always practice gentle speech.
One should exhort others to abide in the path of goodness and give rise to great compassion.
Tenth, eliminate deviant conduct and do not damage the void.
Be firm in your resolve and faith, never shrinking from weariness or suffering.
Constantly exhort others not to abandon them, and aspire to virtuous spiritual friends.
Or, in a pure place such as a forest or a spring, one should give rise to vast and expansive vows.
Be careful not to be timid or weak;
maintain mindfulness at every thought-moment to prevent the arising of wrong views.
Constantly abiding in the Mahāyāna and greeting and prostrating to virtuous spiritual friends—
those who can sever these ten matters possess the realization of the Dharma.
They will certainly proceed directly to unsurpassed bodhi, never again to regress.
"To cultivate the body of a Bodhisattva and a Vajra-body to fulfillment is not difficult.
At that time, having heard this teaching, the Bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
I now practice and study such vows and conduct.
I pray only that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, will proclaim these wondrous and sublime verses.
The great assembly looks up to you with joy and wishes now to receive and uphold them.
The Buddha addressed the sons of good family:
"Speak as you wish to speak; listen attentively, listen attentively.
At that time, the Tathāgata again, by means of the bodhicitta, [spoke].
To protect the great assembly and cause their minds to remain unmoved, he then spoke this mantra:
"The Great Heart-and-Mind Dharani of All Buddhas: Oṃ vara vara saṃvara saṃvara indriya viśuddhe hā ha svāhā. First, with both left and right hands...
Bend the two ring fingers like hooks,
place them behind the middle fingers,
and position the two thumbs [at the base].
Bend each of the two little fingers over their respective nails;
bend each of the two index fingers and hook them around the tips of the two ring fingers.
Straighten the middle fingers of both hands and join the tips of the index fingers;
with the wrists joined against the heart,
the mudrā is formed.
If a person practices this ritual method,
they will attain the bodhicitta and the wisdom of a bodhisattva,
and become fully endowed with all the gateways of the pāramitās.
All that is encompassed within the mind—
namely, all the buddhas, bodhi, and secret gateways—
is subsumed by this seal.
If one receives and maintains this sutra for seven days in a pure chamber,
all essential teachings will appear before one's eyes.
Regarding the paths of all māras, the paths of sentient beings, and the paths of all ghosts and spirits—
If one thus conceals one's form and remains hidden,
by holding this mudrā, the location will naturally become known;
furthermore, even if one wishes to transform one's appearance, such transformation cannot be achieved.
"O sons of good family,
if one obtains this seal,
the Buddhas of the ten directions will immediately gather like clouds above one's crown as soon as it is brought to mind."
As soon as he thinks of it, Bodhisattvas from the ten directions appear, seeking to serve as his attendants;
as soon as he thinks of it, Vajrapāṇis from the ten directions appear, seeking to serve as his personal assistants;
as soon as he thinks of it, devas from the ten directions appear to guard him and provide offerings.
All the retinues of the Māras shall abandon their native lands to assist the majesty of the Dharma;
all the Vināyakas shall come seeking to offer worship.
O sons of good family, those who wish to subdue the māras, enemies,
and non-Buddhists should first form this mudrā and recite the mantra twenty-one times,
then place it upon their hearts.
Turning his body and rising, he circled to the left once;
at that moment, the earth shook violently,
and the hosts of māras were plunged into the subterranean depths from which they never again emerged.
Even if there are those who emerge from it, this is due to the Buddha’s compassionate pity;
yet, one must be careful not to give rise to anger upon emerging.
If those who uphold this mantra give rise to anger, [the benefit will be lost].
The ten directions were turbulent and not at peace;
only now, O sons of good family, have the ten directions begun to settle.
It is the head of all Buddhas, the mother of all dharmas, and the king of all mantras.
All Buddhas of the ten directions are born from it;
like the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, it is without peer.
If you do not master it, you must certainly memorize it and not employ it lightly;
apply it according to the magnitude of the matter.
If you uphold these dharmas...
First, take this mudrā as the foremost.
Without this mudrā, all dharmas lack a master;
even if there were accomplishment, one's entire body and mind would not be stabilized.
The various deities will not protect you, and the dharmas you perform will encounter many obstacles and difficulties.
Be cautious, be cautious! Do not employ them without purity.
Second is the Single Seal of the Accomplishment of Bodhicitta, also known as the Universal Seal of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions; use the aforementioned mantra.
First, with the left and right hands,
interlace the middle fingers such that the right presses upon the left,
with the tips protruding from the "tiger mouth."
The two ring fingers are bent together to press upon the backs of the two middle fingers;
the two thumbs each grasp [the ring fingers].
The two ring fingers are joined at their tips behind;
the two index fingers are joined at their tips on the backs of the two ring fingers;
and the two little fingers are held straight up and pressed together.
When the heads are joined together to form [the seal],
if a son or daughter of good family attains and maintains this mudrā, [they shall obtain such benefits].
By transforming karma and eliminating obstacles, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
By constantly holding this mudrā, one will attain the power of hearing and retaining teachings without forgetfulness,
and will naturally penetrate the essential points of all dharmas.
That which has not been upheld since time immemorial,
all that which is to be performed by the mind shall now be in perfect accord.
At the time of upholding this Dharma, there will be various non-Buddhists as well as Māra Pāpīyān.
Those who come wishing to cause affliction will have their intentions immediately repelled as soon as they raise them.
If there is anything required, they will arrive at the mere touch of a seal.
Even if they manifest a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes, they are unable to delude either persons or the Dharma.
If one binds the seal and maintains the visualization, the deity will manifest its original form.
Regarding treasures hidden in the earth or within the palaces of the nāgas,
whatever one requires, by pointing with the seal, it shall arrive immediately at that very moment.
If one wishes to accomplish any of the essential dharmas existing throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
one should form the mudrā and perform the recitation during the first watch of the night,
without leaving one's original seat.
Then, while in sleep, one will receive all essential dharmas from the worlds of the ten directions;
whatever the mind desires will spontaneously be taught and arrive.
If one seeks minor supernatural powers (*siddhi*), they will be attained within three days.
If one seeks great spiritual penetration, it shall not exceed seven days;
within one's dreams, the Buddha will personally seal the crown of one's head and protect one with his power.
If one desires to behold the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, gods, ghosts, spirits, and Vajras, [they shall appear].
Each time you form the mudrā, seal your eyes with it.
When you reach one thousand and eighty recitations, you will surely see [the deity]; at that point, you must settle your mind.
Do not allow yourself to become frightened or agitated, lest you lose your composure.
If there are various evils, calamities, or disturbances in one's native land,
recite the mantra one hundred and eight times; then,
using the ritual hand-gesture (*mudrā*), point toward the heavens and draw the syllable *Bhrūṃ*.
The calamity will be extinguished immediately and shall not arise again.
If, while holding this mudrā, one is harassed by various māras,
it is sufficient to say "you petty thief" no more than two or three times, and the māra will immediately retreat.
Regarding all the minor ailments of the world, as well as those difficult to cure and hard to identify—
if one merely binds the mudrā and recites the mantra for a full day, even cases of insanity will be eliminated,
provided there is no lack of sincerity.
If one requires any essential Dharma from the Nāga Treasury,
by forming the mudrā, reciting the mantra, and invoking the name of the Nāgarāja,
that Dharma will manifest of its own accord within a single night.
When you see it, you must recite and uphold it without ever forgetting it again.
If you obtain this dharma, keep it strictly secret to yourself.
Do not transmit this to non-humans; be careful, be careful!
If you wish to use this seal to measure the magnitude of matters, perform the rite for great matters.
Do not perform minor rites;
this will diminish their spiritual efficacy.
Take note of this, take note of this!
The third is the *Bodhicittotpāda-mudrā*, also known as the *Sarvaguhyadvāra-saṃgraha-mudrā* or the *Uṣṇīṣa-cakra-mudrā*.
It is employed by all Buddhas alike. First, with both hands:
The ring finger should protrude from between the middle and index fingers.
Next, join the two middle fingers and the two index fingers together with their tips touching.
The four fingers are aligned with their tips touching;
the two thumbs press upon the joints of the upper phalanges of the two index fingers.
Join the two little fingers with their tips together and hold them upright;
join the wrists to form the mudrā.
If there are good sons or others [who practice this],...
Those who wish to uphold the Vajra-mind Dharma of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas should rely on this mudrā;
by recollecting it, they shall immediately attain the immovable wisdom that pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
This is neither saint nor non-saint, neither Māra nor non-Māra.
Together with the celestial immortals, those in the four stages of fruition, and the various great spirits and ghosts,
they simultaneously brought their original minds into perfect accord with one another regarding all worldly affairs.
Discriminating the worldly and discriminating the non-worldly—
from this point on, they immediately harmonize and become one with the Buddha-mind. Why is this?
Because it is by attaining the gateways to the samādhis of all Buddhas;
because the secret treasury of all Buddhas is gathered therein;
and because the uṣṇīṣa-cakras of all Buddhas are accomplished thereby.
Because all vajras abide in accordance with it;
because the multitudes of sages from the ten directions come to take refuge in it;
and because all evils are turned toward the good.
Because all evils are naturally restrained through the gathering of the mind;
because all obstacles are naturally eliminated;
and because the celestial Māra Pāpīyān is naturally subdued.
Because the daughters of the naked ascetics (nirgrantha) who had fallen into error sought his compassion;
because all the dragon treasuries spontaneously opened of their own accord;
and because the various deities of hidden treasures (pātāla-nidhi) spontaneously offered their gifts.
Because the precious jewel of the Dragon King manifests before them,
and because Yama, the Son of Heaven, who is the master over the opening and closing of the five realms of existence,
shall come in person to repent.
All dharmas cannot manifest before one;
yet by relying on this very seal, they do manifest.
This is because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have self-realized the various gates of both the regressive and the progressive.
Because the majestic radiance of all bodhisattvas cannot obstruct the body of this practitioner,
and because all small and great vows and aspirations shall be fulfilled;
if there be any good man or good woman who attains and upholds this seal (mudrā), [they shall likewise achieve these results].
Within this pure mind, be careful not to become confused or distracted;
collect the mind in meditative concentration.
First, recite the Three Refuges and give rise to the intention to receive the precepts.
However, when this seal was bound, at that very moment,
the earth deities of the ten directions appeared.
Holding an incense burner, one makes offerings to this person.
Then Śakra and Brahmā appear before that person and preach the teachings on vows and the methods for holding the mudrās.
The Great Deities stand at the left and right to serve as witnesses;
the Consecrated Universal Monarch and the Vajradhara deities stand before and behind.
With their hands they support the Buddha-armors upon the body of the practitioner.
The Vajragarbhas take their positions in the void and rain down great jewel-flowers to comfort the practitioner.
Even if the Tathāgatas of the ten directions were to abide throughout the ten directions and emit light from their white tufts of hair to illuminate the body of the practitioner,
the transformation Buddhas within that light would hold the Great Dharma-Wheel Seal and seal the practitioner.
Having attained the crown of the seal,
all Buddha-dharmas will be naturally and thoroughly realized.
If one wishes to perform this mudrā, one should burn three kinds of incense.
First, sandalwood; second, olibanum; third, aloeswood—burning each separately, the Buddhas of the three periods of time all appear before one.

If you wish to summon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, the Vajras, the various heavens and earths, the gods and spirits, the sun, moon, and constellations, the five paths of existence, the patrol officials, the officials of destiny, and the inspectors,
bind this mudrā and recite the mantra twenty-one times.
Directing the mind to pervade the ten directions, recite the mantra three times; then all will arrive immediately.

If you wish to summon the treasure-store deities of the ten directions, the nāga-treasuries, and the hidden-treasure spirits (*pātāla-nidhi*), point toward the sky with the mudrā of the seal; they will then appear before you.
If one wishes to command spirits, ghosts, the various Vajra-devas, Bodhisattvas,
and even all those possessing the power of the Way,
one should perform the mudrā and recite the mantra seven times— or twenty-one times— silently with the lips.
It will appear before one at the appropriate time and may be employed at will.
Every day, whether by night or at dawn, one should perform the mudrā and recite [the mantra] up to one thousand times.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions assist them with their own power;
how much more so, then, all other outsiders and insiders who possess various dharmic arts and deceptive illusions?
If one desires to cause those who are afflicted to break free from their suffering, they shall break through various illnesses as soon as they raise their minds.
Within a heart of great compassion, they desire to provide protection without any hesitation;
thus, when those suffering from illness come to seek rescue, they cannot leave that person's side.
Simply by forming this mudrā and speaking these words while attending to the side of the patient,
a noble being will manifest a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) to rescue them from their suffering, and they shall recover.
If you wish to employ this dharma, you must first examine it and maintain mindfulness;
do not employ it while impure.
If you employ it while impure, all things will be obstructed and none will be accomplished.
If any mudrā practice has not been accomplished despite long-term maintenance,
one should bind this seal and recite it a thousand times daily;
within seven days, there is no rite that will not be accomplished.
What is employed will then be free from obstruction.
Record this, record it, and do not transmit it to those who are unworthy.
Practice with diligent effort and earnest aspiration for twenty-one days.
One attains Buddhahood and the state of a Bodhisattva.

The fourth is the Seal of the Mother of the Tathāgatas, also known as the Vajra Mother, the Mother of Bodhisattvas, the Mother of the Teachings of All Buddhas, the Mother of All Dharmas, the Mother of All Seals, the Mother of Maheśvara, the Upholder of Seals, and the Mother of Dhāraṇīs.
First, join the palms of both hands.
Interlace the two little fingers, bending them into the palms,
and hook the two index fingers.
Take the tips of the two little fingers and the two thumbs,
pressing them together against the middle joints of the two index fingers.
The two ring fingers are held upright with their tips touching;
the two middle fingers are also held behind the two ring fingers with their tips touching.
The tips of all four fingers are aligned, and the wrists are joined.
One must sit upon that seat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
One may also verify the efficacy by reciting the aforementioned mantra silently with a low voice.
If there are good sons or good daughters, [who practice this...]
Those who wish to maintain this mudrā should mentally recite the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions seven times,
and only then should they bind this mudrā.
This mudrā should be performed every fifteenth day of the waxing moon;
if one binds this mudrā and maintains it for ten thousand recitations,
all the gateways of sovereign dharmas throughout the worlds of the ten directions will manifest as response-bodies.
Even unto the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
one arrives as soon as it is intended, without further hindrance.
Where all Buddhas abide eternally, there I also abide eternally.
When all Buddhas attain the Way, I also attain the Way;
when all Buddhas deliver sentient beings, I also deliver sentient beings;
as all Buddhas are unimpeded, I am also unimpeded.
As all Buddhas manifest transformation bodies, so do I manifest transformation bodies;
as all Buddhas possess the Dharma-body, so do I possess the Dharma-body;
as all Buddhas emit rays of light, so do I emit rays of light.
As all Buddhas are in tranquil concentration, so am I in tranquil concentration;
as all Buddhas are in samādhi, so am I in samādhi;
as all Buddhas preach the Dharma, so do I preach the Dharma.
The Buddhas do not eat, and I likewise do not eat.
Furthermore, all the various deeds performed by the Buddhas, I am fully capable of performing and accomplishing. Why is this?
Because these constitute the eight kinds of mothers therein,
and because of the eight masteries;
for the Buddhas constantly teach the eight masteries.
I am born from this and have no other source.
Possessing this seal, one can command the sovereign power of the eight directions;
within each and every realm, there are likewise eight directions.
In each and every direction, there are eight kinds of mental concomitants. What are these eight?
First, the mental concomitant of transformation.
Second, compassion that accords with the mind;
third, rescuing from suffering that accords with the mind;
fourth, preaching the Dharma that accords with the mind.
Fifth, the five heinous crimes are brought into accord with mastery, following the mind as one wishes.
Sixth, all essential mantras are gathered so that they come and follow one another, obeying the mind as one desires.
Seventh, all poisons are transformed into goodness.
Having attained the state of the Buddha-body, one is irreversible and acts according to the mind.
Regarding all worldly fruits of retribution and merit,
one can give what is to be given, cut what is to be cut, and cultivate what is to be cultivated.
If it must be established, it is established; if it must be destroyed, it is destroyed—following the mind.
Good sons, within such mental activities that follow the mind, there are hundreds of thousands of *Ganges-sand* instances of activities following the mind that cannot be fully described.
If there are those who seek [this], they need only form the mudrā at dawn and seek it; there is nothing that cannot be pursued.
If this does not bear fruit, then all Buddhas would be speaking falsely.
If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to uphold this mudrā,
or who seek the state of Buddhahood.
Those who seek the rank of a bodhisattva,
those who seek the rank of a vajra-holder,
and those who seek the rank of a celestial deity.
Those who wish to seek rebirth in the ten directions;
those who wish to seek rebirth in the Western Quarter;
and those who wish to seek spontaneous rebirth in the lower direction.
Those who seek to attain mastery over rebirth throughout the ten directions,
and those who seek worldly discernment without deficiency,
should simply contemplate with utmost sincerity, reflecting on their own affairs, and recite this mantra one thousand times every day.
Within seven days, one can arrive there;
once separated from this world, one never returns. Why is this?
It is for the sake of attaining the supernatural powers of a Buddha by becoming identical with the Buddha-body;
for the sake of attaining the compassion of a Buddha by becoming identical with the Buddha-mind;
and for the sake of attaining the vision of a Buddha by becoming identical with the Buddha-eye.
It is to attain the Buddha’s empowerment by sharing in the Buddha’s power;
it is to practice in the world by sharing in the Buddha’s conduct;
and it is to receive the direct seal of the Buddha by attaining the Buddha’s seal.
It is for the sake of attaining the same transformations as all Buddhas;
it is for the sake of attaining the Dharma-body through which all Māras and non-Buddhists are spontaneously subdued. How are they subdued?
Because one sees no two bodies but only one body,
and sees no two Buddhas but only one Buddha,
O son of good family, you should know this mudrā.
